analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to classify workers correctly as employees and penalizes misclassification.
analysis.headline: The bill would have required employers to tell workers whether they are employees or contractors, but it died in committee with no hearing, no vote, and zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies sometimes label workers as independent contractors when the law would treat them as employees. Misclassified workers lose minimum wage, overtime, and unemployment insurance, and the government loses payroll taxes. This bill would have required every employer to tell each worker, in writing, how they were classified, made it illegal to wrongly classify an employee as a contractor, doubled the penalty for wage violations tied to misclassification, and directed the Labor Department to step up audits in industries where misclassification is common. It went to two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are misclassified as independent contractors, losing minimum wage, overtime protections, and unemployment insurance; the honest employers who compete against companies that cut costs through misclassification; and state unemployment funds, which currently miss contributions from unreported wages.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every employer to give each worker a written notice stating whether the worker is classified as an employee or a non-employee, with contact information for the Labor Department and a statement that the worker's wage protections depend on the classification [S3].
Makes it a violation of federal labor law to wrongly classify an employee as a non-employee, and makes it illegal to fire or punish a worker who complains about their classification [S3].
Doubles liquidated damages for employers who violate wage rules and misclassify workers, and raises civil penalties up to $5,000 per worker for repeat or willful violations [S3].

Requires states, as a condition of federal unemployment grants, to audit and investigate employers who are not registered under state law or paying unreported wages, and to impose penalties for misclassification and unreported wages [S3].

Directs Labor Department offices to report misclassification findings to the Wage and Hour Division, which may share them with the IRS, and directs Wage and Hour audits toward industries with frequent misclassification [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that rely on classifying workers as independent contractors would face new notice, recordkeeping, and compliance costs, plus doubled damages and higher penalties when they misclassify workers. Small businesses that legitimately hire independent contractors would bear paperwork costs from the notice requirement.

drawbacks.text: The bill presumes a worker is an employee if the employer failed to give the required written notice, and the employer can only rebut that presumption with clear and convincing evidence, which critics would argue stacks the deck against businesses that simply missed a paperwork deadline [S3].

The notice, recordkeeping, and documentation requirements would impose real administrative costs on small businesses and genuinely self-employed workers, not just companies gaming the classification rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is concrete: misclassification is a widespread practice that strips people of minimum wage, overtime, and unemployment coverage, and this bill attacks it with notices, penalties, and audits. The costs are mostly administrative compliance, but the employee presumption and the doubled-damages provision go further than a narrow anti-abuse bill might need to. The bill's practical weakness was political: with no cosponsors, it had no path forward regardless of its merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, where no hearing or vote ever happened, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson of Florida introduced the bill on July 28, 2017 [S1].
It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was taken after the referrals, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that save money by treating employees as contractors keep the status quo; misclassified workers gain nothing because the bill never moved.

sides.party_line_note: A single House Democrat introduced the bill and no other member, from either party, signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

industries.note: These companies build their business model on classifying drivers and gig workers as independent contractors, which avoids minimum wage, overtime, and payroll taxes. The written classification notice and employee presumption would have made misclassification more costly and litigable.

Firms that supply labor through shell entities or misclassify crews would face doubled damages, higher civil penalties, and referrals from the Labor Department to the IRS, directly hitting a cost advantage they hold over employers who classify correctly.

industries.industry: Unemployment insurance funds and state tax agencies
industries.note: The bill requires states to audit employers paying unreported wages and imposes penalties, recovering unemployment contributions that misclassification currently keeps out of the system.
